fr-pots-de-creme: Place the finely chopped chocolate in a heatproof bowl set over a pot of barely simmering water — the bowl should not touch the water. Stir occasionally until the chocolate is fully melted and perfectly smooth. Alternatively, melt in a microwave in 30-second bursts at 50% power, stirring between each. Remove from heat as soon as the last lumps dissolve — residual heat finishes the job. The melted chocolate should be smooth, glossy, and between 45°C and 50°C.

Combine the heavy cream, whole milk, espresso, and vanilla in a saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until wisps of steam rise and small bubbles form around the very edge of the pan — just below a simmer, around 80°C to 85°C. Do not boil: a boil will scald the milk, encourage curdling when added to the yolks, and dissipate the delicate aromatic compounds of the vanilla. Remove from heat the moment a ring of bubbles appears at the pan's edge.

Whisk the egg yolks and caster sugar in a large bowl until just combined and slightly pale — about 30 seconds of active whisking. Do not whip air into the yolk mixture: the goal is a smooth, uniform liquid that will blend easily with the hot cream, not a foam that will bake to a spongy custard. The sugar should be fully dissolved and no streaks of undissolved sugar should remain. The mixture will be a rich golden-yellow, slightly viscous, and smooth.

Pour the hot infused cream into the yolk mixture in a very thin, slow stream, whisking constantly and gently — the stream should be no wider than a pencil. This gradual warming prevents the yolks from scrambling. When all the cream is incorporated, pour this mixture over the melted chocolate and stir slowly from the centre outward until the custard base is completely smooth and glossy. Add the fleur de sel and stir once. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a pouring jug to remove any cooked egg threads and the espresso grounds. Skim any surface bubbles with a spoon — a bubbly surface bakes to a pocked, matte finish.

Preheat the oven to 150°C (300°F). Arrange small ramekins or oven-safe pots in a deep roasting tin. Pour the custard through the fine sieve once more into the ramekins, filling each to just below the rim. Slide the tin into the oven and pour very hot water into the tin to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Cover the entire tin loosely with foil and bake for 30 to 40 minutes until the custards have set at the edges with a distinct wobble at the centre when the tin is nudged — like a slow, gentle jelly. Remove from the bain-marie, cool to room temperature, then refrigerate uncovered for at least 3 hours before serving. Serve in the pot, directly at the table.
fr-prawn-bisque: Heat a large, heavy-based pot over high heat until smoking. Add half the butter and, when it foams and subsides, add all the prawn shells and heads in a single layer. Press them down firmly with a wooden spoon and do not stir for 60 seconds. The shells will turn vivid coral-red and the tomalley in the heads will burst into fragrant orange fat. Stir and press repeatedly for 4–5 minutes, crushing the heads to release every drop of their orange coral. You are building the bisque's characteristic coral color and deep crustacean flavor entirely at this stage — pale, unroasted shells make a pale, insipid bisque. The pot bottom should develop a golden-orange fond.

Add the remaining butter to the pot with the roasted shells. Add the finely diced onion, celery, carrot, and garlic all at once. Sauté, stirring frequently, for 5–6 minutes until the vegetables are completely softened and beginning to turn golden — they need to be truly soft before the liquid goes in, as the short simmering time won't cook them further. Add the tomato paste and cook, pressing and stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick-red (the pinçage). This caramelization of the tomato paste is essential — it adds sweetness and body, and removes the harsh raw-tomato note.

Remove the pot briefly from heat. Add the cognac and tilt the pot to ignite over a gas flame, or simply return to high heat and let it reduce vigorously for 2 minutes — the alcohol must be cooked off entirely. Scrape every bit of the caramelized fond from the pot bottom with a wooden spoon. Add the white wine and reduce by half over high heat. Add the fish stock or water, bay leaves, thyme, and peppercorns. Bring to a bare simmer. Cook at a gentle simmer for exactly 25 minutes — never boil a shellfish stock hard, as bitter compounds extract from the shells beyond this point. At 25 minutes the stock should be a deep coral-amber and smell intensely of the sea.

Remove the pot from heat. Using a spider or slotted spoon, fish out and discard the bay leaves and thyme sprigs. Pour everything else — shells, vegetables, and all liquid — into a high-powered blender in batches. Blend each batch on maximum power for 60 seconds. The shells will be completely pulverized into the liquid, adding body and the maximum extraction of their flavor. Pass the blended bisque through a fine-mesh strainer set over a clean pot, pressing very firmly on the solids with the back of a ladle to extract every drop. Discard the fibrous shell remnants in the strainer. The strained bisque should be smooth, velvety, and the color of a coral sunset — no grit or shell fragments.

Return the strained bisque to a medium pot over medium heat. Add the double cream and bring to a gentle simmer. Reduce, stirring occasionally, for 5–8 minutes until the bisque coats the back of a spoon in a thin, even layer — this is the nappe consistency. Meanwhile, in a separate small pan, quickly sauté the reserved whole prawn flesh in butter for 90 seconds until just pink and cooked — do not overcook. Season the finished bisque with sea salt, white pepper, and a pinch of cayenne. Taste carefully: the bisque should taste of sweet cream and concentrated ocean, with a lingering savory finish. Ladle into warm bowls, arrange 2–3 sautéed whole prawns in the center of each bowl, and scatter the chives. Serve with gluten-free bread.
fr-prawn-curry: Heat the coconut oil in a wide, shallow pan over high heat until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Add the mustard seeds — stand back, they will pop violently. When the popping slows (about 30 seconds), add the curry leaves — they will splutter dramatically. Fry for 10 seconds until the leaves turn dark green and crisp. This tempering creates the characteristic base of Kerala cuisine.

Add the shallots to the tempered oil and cook over medium-high heat for 5-6 minutes until golden and softening. Add the ginger and garlic and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant. Add the chilli powder and kukum puli. Stir for 1 minute until the oil takes on a vivid red colour from the chilli. The base should be thick and intensely fragrant.

Pour in the coconut milk and stir to combine with the curry base. Bring to a gentle simmer. Add the prawns and cook for exactly 3-4 minutes — no more. The moment all prawns have curled into a C-shape and turned uniformly pink, they are done. A prawn in a D-shape (fully curled) is overcooked. Taste for salt. Serve immediately over steamed rice.
fr-prawn-laksa: If using raw prawn shells, simmer them in the stock for 15 minutes to build a deeper shellfish base. Strain and discard the shells. This step dramatically increases the prawn flavor in the broth and is worth the extra time. If using ready-made prawn stock, skip the shell simmer.

Heat a splash of oil in a deep pot over medium heat. Add the laksa paste and toasted belacan. Fry, stirring constantly, for 3–4 minutes until the paste darkens by one shade, the raw smell burns off, and the oil begins to separate and pool around the edges of the paste. This 'cooking out' step is essential — raw paste tastes sharp and unbalanced.

Pour in the coconut cream and prawn stock. Stir to combine and bring to a gentle simmer — not a rolling boil, which will break the coconut cream and make the broth grainy. Season with fish sauce. Simmer gently for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the broth is fragrant, rich, and just slightly thickened.

Bring the broth to a lively simmer. Add the soaked noodles and poach for 2 minutes until tender. Slide in the raw prawns and cook for exactly 90 seconds until just pink throughout. Remove from heat immediately. Adjust seasoning with lime juice and fish sauce. Ladle into deep bowls over a nest of noodles and prawns. Top with bean sprouts, laksa leaves, and sliced chili.
fr-prawn-saganaki: Heat olive oil in a 25–30 cm oven-safe skillet (preferably cast-iron or a ceramic saganaki dish) over medium heat. Add shallots and cook for 3–4 minutes until softened. Add garlic and chili flakes, stir 30 seconds. Add ouzo — it will flame dramatically if using a gas burner; tilt the pan away from you and let the flames die naturally (about 10 seconds). Pour in the hand-crushed tomatoes and their juices, add oregano and a pinch of sugar. Simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened and darkened slightly. Season with salt and pepper.

Preheat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Nestle the prawns into the bubbling tomato sauce in a single layer, pressing them down gently. Scatter the crumbled feta over and around the prawns in large, irregular chunks — do not crumble it too finely, you want visible pieces that remain distinct when baked. The feta should cover perhaps 60% of the surface, leaving gaps of tomato visible.

Bake at 220°C (425°F) on the top rack for 8–10 minutes. The prawns will turn from grey to pink-orange, the feta will soften but not melt (it holds its shape unlike most cheeses), and the exposed sauce around the edges will bubble and concentrate, possibly catching color on the pan rim. The feta's surface may pick up a touch of golden color.

Bring the pan straight from the oven to the table — saganaki is a tableside experience and must be eaten from the pan while it is still bubbling. Scatter fresh parsley generously over the top. Serve with hunks of gluten-free bread for dragging through the sauce. To eat shell-on prawns: twist off the head (suck it — the inside is extraordinary), peel the body shell, eat.
fr-profiteroles: Combine the water, diced butter, salt, and sugar in a heavy saucepan. Set over medium heat and stir occasionally until the butter melts completely. Increase the heat and bring to a full, rolling boil — every bubble breaking the surface. Do not let it reduce; have the flour ready and act immediately when it boils. A partial boil is not sufficient — the entire liquid must be at a true boil when the flour goes in, or the starch will not cook properly.

Tip all the flour into the boiling liquid at once. Stir immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon — the mixture will seize into a rough, shaggy mass, then smooth out within 30 seconds into a ball. Return to medium heat and continue stirring, pressing the paste against the bottom of the pan, for 1 to 2 minutes to dry it out — a thin skin should form on the pan base. Transfer to a stand mixer bowl or large bowl and beat briefly to cool, then add the beaten eggs in 6 to 8 additions, beating well after each. Stop when the paste falls from the beater in a slow V and holds its shape when piped.

Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F). Pipe the choux paste onto lined baking sheets in rounds of about 3 cm diameter, spaced 5 cm apart. Wet a finger and smooth any peaks. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until puffed, deeply golden brown, and rigid. Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes. After the puffs are golden and holding their shape, reduce the heat to 170°C and bake for a further 5 minutes to dry the interior. Transfer to a rack and pierce the base of each puff with a skewer to release steam. Cool completely before filling.

Heat half the heavy cream in a small saucepan to just below a boil — wisps of steam and a quiver of surface movement, no rolling bubbles. Pour the hot cream over the finely chopped dark chocolate in a heatproof bowl and leave undisturbed for 90 seconds. Stir from the centre outward in slow circles until the ganache is completely smooth and glossy. The sauce should be pourable and warm but not runny — if too thick, add a splash of cream. Keep warm over a pot of hot water.

Using cold cream, cold bowl, and cold beaters, whip the remaining heavy cream with the vanilla extract to firm but not stiff peaks — it should hold its shape when piped but feel airy, not grainy. Transfer to a piping bag. Make a small incision in the base of each puff with a serrated knife and pipe in the cream until the puff feels noticeably heavier. Arrange in a bowl or on a plate, pile generously, and pour the warm chocolate sauce over at the table so guests hear the sauce hitting the cream. Serve immediately.

fr-provencal-tian: Use a mandoline or very sharp knife to slice all vegetables to a uniform 5 mm thickness. Consistency is what makes the tian visually cohesive — irregular slices bake unevenly, leaving raw patches beside overdone edges. Lay slices on a clean surface and assess for uniformity.

Coat the bottom of a wide earthenware gratin dish with a third of the olive oil. Scatter garlic slices across the oil. Arrange the vegetable rounds standing upright in overlapping rows — potato, zucchini, tomato, repeating — tilting each round slightly so it leans on the one behind it. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the top, scatter herbs throughout the slices, and season generously with flaky salt and pepper.

Cover the dish with foil and bake at 180 C (350 F) for 40 minutes to steam the vegetables through. Remove the foil and raise the oven to 220 C (425 F). Bake a further 25–35 minutes until the tops are deeply golden and the tomato has caramelised at its edges. The dish should be bubbling gently at the perimeter. Rest 10 minutes before serving.
fr-pulled-pork-shoulder: Mix all the spices, sugar, and salt together into a uniform rub. Pat the pork shoulder completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture prevents the rub from adhering and forms steam instead of bark during cooking. Apply the rub in a thick, generous, even layer across every surface of the shoulder, pressing and patting it in firmly. Do not neglect any surface, including the fat cap and under any folds. Wrap the rubbed shoulder in plastic wrap or place in a large zipper bag and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, ideally overnight (12 hours). The salt in the rub draws out moisture, dissolves into a brine, and is reabsorbed — seasoning the meat deeply rather than just the surface.

Set up the smoker or grill for indirect heat at a stable temperature of 107 to 120 C / 225 to 250 F. This is the low-and-slow window — above 135 C / 275 F the exterior dries before the interior collagen has had time to dissolve. Add hardwood chunks to the fire: oak and hickory are traditional for a bold, Southern BBQ character; apple and cherry are milder and pair beautifully with pork's sweetness. Place the shoulder fat-cap side up on the grate over the indirect zone. Smoke for 6 to 8 hours, maintaining the temperature window and adding wood as needed. Spritz with apple cider vinegar every 90 minutes after the first 3 hours to keep the surface moist and promote bark formation without washing the rub away.

Once the bark is fully formed and the internal temperature is between 74 and 82 C / 165 and 180 F, wrap the shoulder tightly in two layers of heavy-duty foil (the Texas Crutch). Add a small splash of apple cider vinegar into the foil before sealing. Return to the smoker at the same temperature. The foil traps moisture and steam, rapidly converting remaining collagen to gelatin and driving the internal temperature through the stall. Cook until the internal temperature reaches 95 to 97 C / 203 to 207 F — the bone-probe temperature. At this temperature, the probe or a skewer should slide into the meat with the resistance of soft butter.

Transfer the wrapped shoulder (still in its foil) to a clean, empty cooler. Close the cooler and rest for a minimum of 1 hour, ideally 2 hours. This rest is not optional — it is what transforms the shoulder from simply cooked to superlative. During the rest, the internal temperature equalizes, the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb their juices, and the collagen that converted to gelatin coats every fiber, making the final pull glossy and self-saucing. A properly rested shoulder held in a cooler maintains temperature for up to 4 hours, so you can rest it comfortably while preparing everything else.

Pull the pork using two forks or your hands (with clean heat-resistant gloves). Start from the bone and work outward, pulling the meat apart into long, natural strands — follow the grain of the muscle. Avoid chopping or shredding too finely; long, silky strands are the ideal. Pour the collected resting juices over the pulled meat and toss to coat. Chop the darkest pieces of bark into small bits and fold them through the pulled meat — these dark, intensely flavored bits are called 'burnt ends adjacent' and are prized for the concentrated spice-smoke flavor they add to the final mix. Taste and add salt or a splash of apple cider vinegar if needed.
fr-puls: Rinse the emmer in cold water until it runs clear, then cover it generously with part of the water and leave it overnight, 8 hours or more. Whole emmer is a tough, hulled grain; the long soak rehydrates the bran and lets the kernels swell so they will cook down sweet and tender rather than staying chalky at the core. Reserve the rest of the water for the cook.

Put the drained emmer in a heavy pot with the reserved water and the salt. Bring to a boil, then drop to the barest simmer and cook uncovered, stirring often as it thickens, 45 minutes to over an hour depending on the grain. As the kernels burst they release starch and the pot turns from soupy to a thick, spoon-coating pottage. Add hot water as needed; you want the grains broken and creamy, not dry. Salting now seasons from within as the starch absorbs the liquid.

Off the heat, beat in the olive oil and most of the grated cheese until the puls turns glossy and rich; the residual heat melts the cheese into the starch for savory depth. Stir through the chopped lovage and a heavy grind of pepper. Taste and correct the salt. Spoon into bowls, scatter the remaining cheese over the top, and finish with a thread of olive oil — or, for the full Roman effect, a few drops of garum.

fr-pumpkin-pie: If using a raw pie shell, line it with parchment and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake at 190°C for 15 minutes. Remove weights and parchment and bake a further 5 minutes until the base is just set and dry, but not browned. This par-baking prevents the classic soggy bottom. Cool slightly before filling.

In a separate bowl, whisk the eggs and extra yolk until smooth, then add the heavy cream and whisk to combine. Pour the egg-cream mixture into the pumpkin mixture and whisk until completely smooth. Do not over-whisk or you will incorporate air that causes cracking during baking.

Pour the custard into the par-baked shell, filling to within 5mm of the top edge. Tent the crust edges with foil or a pie shield. Bake at 165°C for 50–60 minutes until the edges of the custard are set but the center 5cm still jiggles when the pie is gently shaken. Remove and cool completely at room temperature for 2 hours, then refrigerate.

Cool the pie on a wire rack at room temperature for 2 full hours. Do not refrigerate immediately — rapid temperature change causes cracking. After 2 hours, refrigerate uncovered for at least 2 hours before slicing. The filling must be completely cold before cutting — warm pumpkin pie filling is still technically liquid and will collapse when cut.

fr-quinoa-tabbouleh: Rinse the quinoa under cold running water for a full 60 seconds in a fine-mesh sieve, rubbing the grains between your palms. This removes the bitter saponin coating. Combine with the water in a small saucepan and bring to a boil over medium heat. Reduce to the lowest simmer, cover, and cook 12–14 minutes until all water is absorbed. Remove from heat and let steam, covered, for 5 minutes. Then tip onto a large tray or baking sheet and spread into a thin layer to cool completely to room temperature — adding warm quinoa to the salad will wilt the herbs and cook the vegetables.

The knife work here makes or breaks tabbouleh. Strip the parsley leaves from their stems (save stems for stock) and chop very finely — almost to a near-paste in texture, not a rough chop. The mint should be treated the same way. Dice the seeded tomatoes and cucumber to a uniformly fine dice, roughly 5mm. Slice the scallions thinly, including most of the green tops. Tabbouleh is a parsley salad with other ingredients; if the quinoa is dominant, you've made a grain bowl. Parsley should be the visual and volumetric majority.

In a large bowl, combine the cooled quinoa with the chopped herbs, tomatoes, cucumber and scallions. Drizzle over the lemon juice and olive oil, season with salt and pepper, and toss gently but thoroughly. Taste and adjust — authentic tabbouleh is assertively lemony and well-salted; it should make your eyes water slightly with the brightness of lemon. Let rest at room temperature for 10–15 minutes before serving — this brief rest allows the quinoa to absorb the dressing and the flavors to marry.
fr-red-beans-and-rice: Melt the butter in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion, celery, and green bell pepper — the holy trinity of Creole cooking. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until softened and beginning to turn translucent. Add the garlic and cook 1 more minute. Push the vegetables to the sides and add the sliced Andouille sausage in a single layer. Let the sausage brown for 2–3 minutes per side without moving it — you want a rendered crust that will give the beans their smoky depth. Stir everything together.

Add the drained, soaked kidney beans to the pot. Add bay leaves, thyme, cayenne, smoked paprika, and a generous pinch of salt. Cover with cold water by 5 cm. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered or loosely covered for 1.5–2 hours, stirring every 20 minutes and adding water to keep the beans just submerged. After 90 minutes, begin mashing a few beans against the side of the pot with the back of a spoon — these crushed beans will thicken the pot liquor to a creamy, gravy-like consistency. Continue until the pot liquid is thick and creamy and the beans are completely tender. Taste for salt, cayenne, and smoke.

While the beans finish, cook the rice in a separate saucepan. Rinse the rice until the water runs almost clear. Combine with cold water in a 1:1.75 ratio, add a pinch of salt, and bring to a boil. Reduce to the lowest possible heat, cover tightly, and cook for 15 minutes. Remove from heat and rest covered for 10 minutes without lifting the lid. Fluff with a fork. The rice should be separate, fluffy, and dry enough to soak up the bean gravy.

Scoop a mound of fluffy white rice into the center of each bowl. Ladle the red beans and sausage generously over and around the rice so the creamy gravy puddles at the base. The classic ratio is roughly equal parts rice and beans in the bowl. Garnish with sliced scallion and a few dashes of Louisiana hot sauce if desired. The beans will continue to thicken as the dish sits — this is traditional and desirable.
fr-red-braised-pork: Place the pork belly cubes in a cold pot. Cover with cold water by 5 cm — starting in cold water draws the blood and impurities out gradually, rather than sealing them in. Bring to a boil over high heat. You will see grey-white foam rising to the surface within 4–5 minutes; this is myoglobin and blood protein coagulating. Once the water reaches a rolling boil and the foam is substantial, drain the pork immediately into a colander. Rinse each cube under warm running water, rubbing off any clinging foam with your fingers. Do not use cold water — a sudden temperature drop can tighten the proteins and make the pork less tender. Pat dry with paper towels. This step is non-negotiable: skipping it results in a muddy, gray braising liquid instead of the clean, lacquered mahogany sauce that defines hong shao rou.

In a wide, heavy-bottomed wok or Dutch oven, heat the oil over medium heat. Add the rock sugar and stir slowly with a wooden spatula as it melts — rock sugar is slow to melt compared to granulated sugar, and patience matters here. The sugar will first form clear, bubbling puddles, then turn pale gold, then amber. Watch the color carefully: you want a deep amber, the color of dark honey, before adding the pork. This caramelized sugar is what gives hong shao rou its characteristic mahogany color and bitter-sweet depth that soy sauce alone cannot replicate. Remove from heat if it darkens too quickly — the residual heat in a wok can tip amber into burnt very fast.

Add the dry pork cubes to the hot caramel. The sugar will spit aggressively — use a splatter screen or step back. Toss the pork to coat it in the caramel. The skin side is the most important: press it face-down into the caramel for 1–2 minutes until it takes on a deep mahogany stain. Turn the cubes on all sides until they are uniformly coated and darkened to a rich brown. The pork fat will start to render, mixing with the caramel. This sealing-and-coloring phase takes 4–5 minutes total. Add the ginger slices, scallion knot, star anise, and cassia bark and toss for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Pour the Shaoxing wine around the edges of the wok, letting it sizzle and release its alcohol in a fragrant cloud — do not pour it directly onto the pork, as this can cool the meat and stop the caramelization. Add the dark soy, light soy, and water or stock. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the pork, never fully covering it. Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer you can manage — just a gentle bubble at the surface, not a rolling boil. Cover with a lid slightly ajar. Braise for 1 hour 30 minutes, turning the pork every 30 minutes so all sides spend time submerged. The slow, gentle heat is what converts collagen to gelatin and transforms the fat from solid and waxy to trembling and yielding. After 90 minutes, remove the lid and taste the braising liquid — it should already be complex and slightly sweet.

Remove the lid completely. Increase the heat to medium-high. The braising liquid, which is now rich with gelatin and soy, will begin to reduce rapidly. Stir and baste the pork every 2–3 minutes, spooning the liquid over the top surfaces. As the sauce reduces, it will transition from a thin, glossy broth to a syrupy lacquer that coats the back of a spoon. The pork will simultaneously deepen in color from mahogany to an almost black-red glaze. This stage takes 15–25 minutes depending on the volume of liquid remaining. Watch carefully in the last 5 minutes — the sauce can go from perfect to burnt very quickly as the sugar concentration increases. Remove the star anise, cassia, ginger, and scallion knot. The sauce is ready when it coats the pork in a thick, shiny layer that holds for several seconds before slowly dripping.

fr-refried-beans: Rinse beans and place in a large pot with water, quartered onion, and epazote. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer. Cook uncovered for 2-2.5 hours, adding hot water as needed to keep the beans submerged. Do not salt until the last 30 minutes — early salt toughens the skins. The beans are done when they crush effortlessly between your fingers.

Heat lard in a wide, heavy skillet over medium heat. When it shimmers, add the diced onion. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft, golden, and sweet — about 8 minutes. The onion-flavored fat is the foundation of the refried beans' richness.

Add the cooked beans to the skillet in batches, mashing them into the onion-fat mixture with a potato masher or the back of a large wooden spoon. Add splashes of the reserved bean broth to keep the mixture moist. Work in batches — fry, mash, add more beans. The beans should sizzle and fry as they are mashed, not just be stirred in.

Season with salt to taste. Continue cooking over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for another 3-5 minutes. The beans will tighten and become glossy. They should be thick enough to hold a spoon upright but still spreadable — like soft sunflower seed butter. Adjust with bean broth if too thick.
fr-rendang: Drain the soaked dried chilies. Combine all paste ingredients — dried chilies, fresh chilies, shallots, garlic, galangal, ginger, and fresh turmeric — in a blender or food processor. Add a splash of water (2–3 tablespoons) to help the blades catch. Blend to a smooth, fine paste, scraping down the sides several times. The paste should have the consistency of thick hummus with no visible chunks of shallot or galangal remaining. Taste it raw: it should be fiercely aromatic, bright with chili, and pungent with allium. This is the rempah — the soul of the rendang.

Heat the oil in a large, wide, heavy pot or wok over medium heat. Add the rempah paste, lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, and turmeric leaves. Fry, stirring almost constantly, for 12–18 minutes. The paste will sputter and pop, then slowly darken and begin to stick to the pot. Keep stirring — this constant movement prevents burning and drives off the raw moisture in the aromatics. The rempah is ready when it has darkened several shades to a deep brick-red, the oil begins to separate and pool around the paste, and the kitchen fills with a toasted, fragrant aroma rather than the sharp raw smell of the uncooked paste.

Add the beef chunks to the fried rempah and stir to coat every surface. Pour in the coconut milk, add the salt and palm sugar, and stir to combine. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a vigorous simmer. The liquid will be a pale orange-yellow. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally at first and more frequently as the liquid reduces. After about 1.5 to 2 hours, most of the liquid will have evaporated. Add the kerisik (toasted coconut) now — it absorbs the remaining liquid, thickens the sauce, and adds a nutty richness. Continue cooking.

Once the sauce is thick and the oil has separated, lower the heat slightly and continue cooking, now stirring almost constantly. The liquid is essentially gone and the beef is beginning to fry in the released coconut and spice oil. This final stage is transformative and takes another 30–60 minutes of patient, attentive stirring. The sauce will coat the meat in a dark, almost-black crust, and the aroma will shift from a curried fragrance to something deeper, drier, and almost smoky. The pot will hiss and crackle. This is rendang becoming rendang. Taste and adjust salt. Serve with steamed rice.
fr-ribollita: Drain the soaked beans and cover with fresh cold water by 5 cm in a large pot. Add the herb bundle and a generous pinch of salt. Bring to a boil, skim any grey foam that rises, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 60-90 minutes until the beans are completely tender throughout with no chalky center when bitten. Do not add acid (no tomato, no vinegar) until the beans are fully cooked — acid toughens bean skins. Reserve all the cooking liquid — it becomes the base of the soup. Remove the herb bundle. Roughly mash or blend one-third of the cooked beans directly in the pot to create body in the soup; leave two-thirds whole.

In a separate large, heavy pot, heat the olive oil over medium-low heat. Add the onion, celery, carrot, and garlic with a pinch of salt. Cook slowly for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are completely soft, sweet-smelling, and lightly golden. This is the soffritto — the flavor foundation. The vegetables should be so soft they break apart when pressed with a spoon. Add the crushed tomatoes, stir in, and cook for another 5 minutes until the tomato has darkened slightly and smells sweet.

Add the cavolo nero leaves to the soffritto and stir until wilted, about 3 minutes. Pour in the cooked beans along with all their cooking liquid. Add more water or stock if needed — the mixture should be soupy, not stew-thick. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 25-30 minutes until the cavolo nero is completely tender and has lost its tough, fibrous quality. The broth should taste deeply savory and slightly sweet from the beans. Season generously with salt and pepper.

Tear the stale bread into large, rough chunks — about 5 cm pieces — and press them into the simmering soup. Do not stir immediately. Let the bread absorb the broth for 2-3 minutes, then stir gently to incorporate. The bread will swell dramatically and begin to fall apart, thickening the soup to a porridge-like consistency. Add more broth if the mixture becomes too thick to stir. Simmer for another 15-20 minutes on low heat, stirring regularly to prevent the bread from sticking to the bottom.

This is the step that gives ribollita its name — 're-boiled.' Bring the thick soup back to a lively simmer over medium heat, stirring frequently to prevent the bread-thickened base from scorching on the bottom. Simmer for 10 minutes. Taste and adjust salt generously — ribollita needs bold seasoning. Ladle into deep bowls. Finish each bowl with a generous pour of the best olive oil you have — it will pool on the surface and slowly sink in. Serve with a coarse grind of black pepper and, optionally, a slice of grilled bread across the top.

The salt ratio is 12 g per kg of meat — precise seasoning is critical since the rillettes will be eaten cold and unseasoned fat is bland. If time allows, cover and refrigerate overnight to let the cure penetrate. Minimum 2 hours.

Place the seasoned pork in a heavy cast-iron or enamel pot. Add the lard, bouquet garni, and white wine. The fat should come roughly halfway up the pork. Cook in a 130 C (265 F) oven, uncovered, for 3.5–4.5 hours, turning the pork pieces gently every hour. The liquid will reduce and the fat will become clear. The pot should maintain a very lazy bubble — almost no movement at the surface.

Remove the bouquet garni and lift the pork pieces into a large bowl with a slotted spoon, reserving all the cooking fat. While the pork is still warm, use two forks to pull it apart into long, rough fibers — not a fine paste, but coarse shreds where individual fibers are visible. Ladle enough of the warm, strained cooking fat back over the shredded meat to moisten it generously and bind it into a spreadable mass. Taste and adjust salt. It should taste aggressively seasoned.

Pack the rillettes firmly into sterilized glass crocks or ramekins, pressing down to eliminate air pockets. Pour a thin layer of the remaining strained fat over the top — this is the preserving seal. Allow to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate uncovered until the fat cap has set completely. Once set, the rillettes will keep refrigerated for 2 weeks. Serve at room temperature with gluten-free bread and cornichons.
fr-risotto-parmigiano: Melt half the butter in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-low heat. Add the diced onion and cook slowly, stirring occasionally, until completely soft and translucent. This takes 8-10 minutes. The onion must never color — the risotto's purity depends on it.

Add the rice to the sweated onion and increase heat to medium. Stir constantly, coating every grain in butter. Toast for 2-3 minutes until the edges of the grains become translucent while the centers remain chalky white. This seals the exterior starch and creates the signature al-dente core.

Add warm stock one ladle at a time, stirring gently but constantly. Wait until each addition is nearly absorbed before adding the next. The rice should always be moist but never swimming. This process takes 16-18 minutes. Taste at 15 minutes — the rice should be tender with the faintest chalky resistance at the core.

Remove the pan from heat. Add the remaining cold butter and the grated Parmigiano. Stir vigorously for 60 seconds — this is the mantecatura, the act of beating the risotto into a creamy emulsion. The cold butter and cheese create a glossy, flowing sauce that binds everything. Season with salt. Cover and rest for 2 minutes.
fr-roast-chicken: Remove the chicken from the refrigerator 1 hour before roasting. Pat it thoroughly dry inside and out with paper towels. Season generously inside the cavity and over every surface of the skin with salt. Set it on a rack over a tray and let it sit uncovered — the air-drying tightens the skin and the salt draws out surface moisture. Dry skin is the path to crisp skin.

Rub the softened butter over the entire surface of the chicken, working it into every crevice — under the wings, between the thighs, and over the back. Season with pepper. Stuff the cavity with the lemon halves and thyme sprigs. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine and tuck the wing tips under the body. The trussing creates a compact shape that roasts evenly.

Place the chicken breast-side up in a roasting pan or cast-iron skillet. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 55-70 minutes, depending on size. Do not open the oven for the first 30 minutes. After that, baste once with the rendered pan juices. The chicken is done when the juices from the thigh run clear and the internal temperature reaches 74 C (165 F) at the thickest part of the thigh.

Transfer the chicken to a cutting board and tent loosely with foil. Rest for 15-20 minutes. This is not optional — resting allows the juices to redistribute from the exterior back into the center of the meat. A rested chicken loses a tablespoon of juice when carved. An unrested one loses a quarter cup.

Remove the twine. Separate the legs by cutting through the joint where the thigh meets the body. Separate thigh from drumstick. Carve the breast by slicing along the breastbone, then angling the knife to follow the ribcage. Arrange on a warm platter and spoon the collected pan juices over each piece.
fr-roast-pork-loin-fennel-apples: Pat the pork dry. Score the fat cap in a shallow crosshatch about 2 cm apart, cutting through the fat but not into the meat. Mix 13 g of the salt with the fennel seed, pepper, garlic, rosemary, and 15 ml of the olive oil into a paste and rub it all over, working it into the scores. Rest uncovered at room temperature 45 minutes to 1 hour (or refrigerate up to 24 hours, then give it 45 minutes out of the fridge). If the roast is untied, tie it with kitchen twine every 4 cm to keep an even cylinder.

Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Heat 15 ml of oil in a large ovenproof skillet or flameproof roasting pan over medium-high heat. Sear the pork fat-side down first for 4–5 minutes, until the fat is golden and rendering, then brown the other sides 2 minutes each. Remove to a plate.

Toss the fennel, apples, and onion with the remaining 15 ml oil and the remaining 3 g salt, and spread in the pan (or a 23 × 33 cm / 9 × 13 in roasting pan). Set the pork fat-side up on top. Roast 50–70 minutes until an instant-read thermometer in the center of the roast reads 145°F (63°C). Start checking at 45 minutes. Move the pork to a board, tent loosely with foil, and rest 15 minutes — the temperature will rise a few degrees and the juices settle.

Move the vegetables and apples to a platter. Set the roasting pan over medium-high heat, pour in the cider, and scrape up the browned bits. Boil 4–6 minutes until reduced by about half. Whisk in the mustard, then take off the heat and swirl in the cold butter until glossy. Add any resting juices from the board. Slice the pork 1 cm thick and serve over the fruit with the sauce spooned on top.

Do not peel — the skin protects the flesh and prevents moisture loss, and it will slip off effortlessly after roasting. Place each beet on a square of foil, add a thyme sprig, a drizzle of olive oil, and a pinch of salt. Wrap tightly into individual parcels. If roasting both red and golden/Chioggia beets, keep them in separate parcels — red beet juice bleeds aggressively and will stain all the others crimson. Roast for 45–60 minutes, depending on size, until a thin knife enters with zero resistance.

When the beets are cool enough to handle but still quite warm, peel them: hold each one in a folded paper towel and rub — the skin should slide off in large sheets under gentle pressure, revealing the gleaming flesh beneath. Wear gloves if working with red beets or expect deeply stained hands. Peel while warm because the skin adheres more stubbornly as the beet cools. Slice or wedge the peeled beets according to preference — thin slices (5mm) for an elegant, layered presentation, or wedges for a more rustic look. Reserve any juice in the foil parcels for the vinaigrette.

In a small bowl, combine the sherry vinegar, Dijon mustard, honey, and finely minced shallot. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper. Whisk vigorously to combine and dissolve the mustard. Then add the olive oil in a slow, steady drizzle while whisking constantly — the mustard acts as an emulsifier and will help the dressing stay together rather than separating into oil and vinegar layers. Taste and adjust: it should be assertively tart (more vinegar), pleasantly sweet (more honey), and pungent from the mustard. Add any reserved beet juices from the foil for depth.

Toast the roughly chopped walnuts in a dry skillet over medium heat, tossing constantly, for 3–4 minutes until they are evenly golden, fragrant, and the oils have activated. Alternatively, toast on the baking tray alongside the beets for the final 5 minutes of roasting. Walnuts move from raw to perfect to burnt in a very short window — constant motion and attention are required. Transfer to a cool plate immediately when done. Season lightly with flaky salt while hot.

Dress the arugula with about one-third of the vinaigrette and toss to coat the leaves lightly. Arrange on a large, wide plate or individual plates. Lay the beet slices or wedges over the greens, alternating colors for visual effect. Drizzle more vinaigrette directly over the beets. Crumble the goat cheese in generous irregular pieces across the surface — do not press it flat. Scatter the toasted walnuts. Finish with the orange zest, a final drizzle of vinaigrette, flaky salt, and a few grinds of black pepper. Serve within 10 minutes of assembly.

fr-roasted-beets: Pour half the coarse salt into a deep baking dish to create a 2 cm bed. Nestle the whole, unpeeled beets on the salt, spacing them so they do not touch. Pour the remaining salt over and around the beets to cover them completely — they should be fully buried with no beet surface visible. The salt draws moisture out slowly and creates a sealed, even-temperature cooking environment, concentrating sugars far more than conventional roasting.

Roast in a preheated 190 C (375 F) oven for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours. The salt will partially harden into a crust. To test for doneness, push a thin metal skewer through the salt into the largest beet — it should pass through with no resistance, like pushing into room-temperature butter. Small beets take 80 minutes; very large ones may need 2 hours 15 minutes.

Crack the salt crust with a spoon and remove the beets. The skin will peel off in large pieces using just your fingers and a paper towel (wear gloves if you don't want to stain your hands deep red for a day). Slice, quarter, or serve whole. Dress immediately with olive oil and a few drops of red wine vinegar or balsamic to add brightness to the concentrated sweetness.

Spread on a large sheet pan with cut sides down and space between pieces. Roast 25–30 minutes, flipping once at 15 minutes, until tender and well charred at the edges.

While the cauliflower roasts, put the lentils, bay leaf, and the smashed garlic clove in a saucepan with the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cook 20–25 minutes until tender but holding their shape. Salt the water in the last 5 minutes. Drain, discard the bay and garlic.

Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, the grated garlic clove, and a pinch of salt. It will seize and thicken — keep going. Add the ice water a tablespoon at a time, whisking until it lightens to a smooth, pourable sauce.

Toss the warm lentils with half the tahini sauce, the remaining 15 ml olive oil, the lemon zest, and half the parsley. Season with salt. Spread on a platter, top with the roasted cauliflower, drizzle over the remaining tahini, and finish with almonds and the rest of the parsley.
fr-roasted-cauliflower-tahini-lentils-nf: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss the florets with 45 ml of the oil, the cumin, paprika, and 1 teaspoon salt. Spread on a large sheet pan with cut sides down and space between pieces. Roast 25–30 minutes, flipping once at 15 minutes, until tender and well charred at the edges.

While the cauliflower roasts, put the lentils, bay leaf, and the smashed garlic clove in a saucepan with the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cook 20–25 minutes until tender but holding their shape. Salt the water in the last 5 minutes. Drain, discard the bay and garlic.

Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, the grated garlic clove, and a pinch of salt. It will seize and thicken — keep going. Add the ice water a tablespoon at a time, whisking until it lightens to a smooth, pourable sauce.

Toss the warm lentils with half the tahini sauce, the remaining 15 ml olive oil, the lemon zest, and half the parsley. Season with salt. Spread on a platter, top with the roasted cauliflower, drizzle over the remaining tahini, and finish with sunflower seeds and the rest of the parsley.
fr-roasted-cauliflower: Bring a large, deep pot of water to a rolling boil and season it aggressively with the kosher salt and the juice of half the lemon — it should taste like seawater. Lower the trimmed whole head in stem-side down, cover, and simmer 8 to 12 minutes. This seasons the cauliflower to its core and softens the dense stem so it cooks through before the surface scorches in the oven. Lift it out carefully with two slotted spoons or a spider and set it stem-down on a rack to drain and steam-dry completely.

Whisk the olive oil with the garlic paste, cumin, and smoked paprika into a loose, rust-colored slurry. Set the drained head in an oven-proof skillet or on a lined sheet and massage the spiced oil over every surface, working it down into the crevices between florets and over the cut stem. Be generous — the oil is both the seasoning and the frying medium that crisps the crown.

Roast in a hot oven at 220C / 425F for 30 to 40 minutes, basting once or twice with the oil that collects in the pan. The Maillard browning turns the surface curds deeply golden and concentrates the sugars into a nutty, almost popcorn sweetness. The head is done when the crown is bronzed and crackly and a skewer slides through the center without resistance.

Transfer the rested head to a warm platter. Squeeze over the juice of the remaining lemon half, scatter with flaky salt and a few grinds of black pepper, then shower with chopped parsley and toasted pine nuts. Bring it whole to the table and carve into thick wedges from the crown down through the tender stem, spooning the spiced pan oil over each portion.

fr-roasted-root-vegetables: Peel all vegetables. Cut into pieces of approximately equal size and similar surface area so they roast at the same rate — this is the single most important prep step. Parsnips halved lengthwise; carrots halved or quartered depending on size; beetroot into 6–8 wedges. Toss in a large bowl with the oil, coating every surface — do not season with salt yet, as salt draws moisture and creates steam in the early roasting stage.

Preheat the oven to 220°C (430°F) with a large, heavy roasting tray inside. The preheated tray is essential — vegetables placed in a cold tray steam rather than roast. Spread the vegetables in a single layer with the cut sides down, with space between each piece — touching vegetables steam each other. Scatter thyme and bay leaves throughout. Roast for 25 minutes without opening the oven.

Turn each piece over to expose an unbrowned side. Season now with flaky sea salt and black pepper. Drizzle honey or maple syrup over the pieces in the tray. Return to the oven for 15–20 more minutes until everything is tender, deeply caramelized, and the honey has darkened and concentrated. The sugar in the glaze accelerates the Maillard reaction on the freshly exposed surfaces.
fr-roasted-tomato-soup: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Divide tomatoes (cut-side up), onion, pepper, and garlic between two rimmed sheet pans, drizzle with oil, sprinkle with the salt, and tuck in thyme sprigs. Roast 45–55 minutes, rotating the pans halfway, until the tomatoes are slumped and blackened in spots and the garlic is soft.

Squeeze the garlic from its skins and discard the skins and thyme stems. Scrape everything into a 5 litre pot, pour a little of the stock onto the hot pans to loosen the stuck juices, and add it all with the remaining stock and the basil. Simmer 10 minutes to marry the flavors.

Blend until smooth with an immersion blender (or in batches in a vented blender). For a silkier soup, press through a sieve to remove skins. Stir in vinegar, then taste: add a pinch of sugar only if it's sharp, and adjust salt. Stir in cream and warm gently without boiling. To freeze: freeze before adding cream (dairy can separate) — cool quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours, freeze up to 4 months, then add cream after reheating.
fr-rum-baba: In a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine flour, sugar, salt, and instant yeast. Add the warm milk and then the eggs one at a time with the mixer running on medium. Beat for 8–10 minutes until the batter is smooth, shiny, and elastic, pulling cleanly away from the bowl sides. The mixture is wetter than a bread dough — closer to a thick batter.

With the mixer running on medium-low, add the very soft butter one tablespoon at a time. Wait until each addition is fully incorporated before adding the next — this takes patience, about 15 minutes total. The batter will loosen dramatically at first, then tighten into a smooth, glossy, enriched dough that pulls cleanly from the bowl.

Cover the bowl and let the dough proof at room temperature until doubled, 45–60 minutes. Then butter individual baba molds (or a muffin tin) generously. Fill each mold halfway with batter using a piping bag or spoon. Let proof again until the dough crests just above the rim, 20–30 minutes.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 18–22 minutes until deeply golden on top and pulling away from the mold sides. A skewer inserted in the center should come out clean. Turn onto a rack immediately and let cool for 15 minutes before soaking — they must be warm but not hot.

Combine water, caster sugar, honey, and the vanilla pod in a wide, shallow saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar and honey dissolve completely. Simmer 2 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the rum. Keep the syrup warm — it must be hot when the babas are soaked.

Place the warm babas into the wide pan of warm syrup (having added the rum to the syrup base). Spoon syrup over continuously, turning the babas, for 2–3 minutes until each one has absorbed the maximum syrup it can hold. A fully soaked baba should feel waterlogged and heavy, and syrup should run from it when pressed gently.

Combine the very cold heavy cream with a small amount of sugar and vanilla extract (if using extract rather than pod) in a chilled bowl. Whip to soft, billowing peaks — Chantilly for baba should be cloud-light, not stiff or butter-like.

Place each soaked baba on a shallow plate. Spoon or pipe a generous dome of Chantilly cream directly on top. Drizzle any remaining warm rum syrup around the base. Serve immediately while the baba is warm and the cream is cold — the contrast is essential.
fr-saag-aloo: Place the cubed potatoes in a saucepan of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8–10 minutes until just tender — a skewer meets slight resistance at the center. Drain and allow the steam to escape for 2 minutes so the surface dries slightly.

Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy pan over high heat until shimmering and a mustard seed dropped in skips and pops. Add the mustard seeds — cover immediately and let them pop for 30 seconds. Reduce heat to medium, add cumin seeds and let sizzle for 15 seconds. Add onion and cook, stirring, until deep golden and beginning to crisp at the edges, 10–12 minutes. Add ginger, garlic, green chili, and turmeric; cook 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears.

Add the spinach in large handfuls to the pan, stirring between each addition until each batch wilts before adding the next. Once all spinach is wilted (about 3 minutes), transfer half of it to a blender or use a hand blender to blitz it to a smooth, vivid-green purée — leave the other half whole for texture. Return the purée to the pan. Add the parboiled potatoes, garam masala, and salt. Stir gently to coat, then simmer on low heat for 5 minutes so the potatoes absorb the sauce. Taste and adjust salt.
fr-saag-paneer: Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a fierce rolling boil. Add all the spinach at once — it will seem like an enormous volume, but it collapses dramatically. Push the spinach below the surface and cook for exactly 2 minutes: no more, or it will lose its vivid green color and turn a muddy army-green. Immediately drain and plunge into a bowl of ice-cold water, holding for 1 full minute to arrest all cooking. Lift the spinach from the cold water and squeeze firmly with both hands to remove as much liquid as possible — excess water will thin the final sauce. Transfer to a blender and blitz until completely smooth, about 2 minutes, adding just 2–3 tablespoons of the blanching water if the blade struggles. The puree should be electric green and pourable.

Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the cumin seeds and let them crackle and darken for 20 seconds. Add the onion and cook, stirring frequently, for 10–12 minutes until it is deeply golden and caramelized at the edges — do not rush this step; the sweetness of properly browned onion forms the flavor backbone of the entire dish. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 2 more minutes until the raw smell vanishes and the mixture turns a pale golden paste. Add the ground coriander, cumin, chili powder, and turmeric; stir constantly for 90 seconds, toasting the ground spices in the fat without letting them scorch. The masala is ready when the fat separates visibly around the edges of the spice mixture — an old cook's signal called 'bhunoing' that the rawness has been driven off.

Pour the spinach puree into the hot masala base — it will sputter and steam dramatically. Stir to combine thoroughly and reduce the heat to medium-low. Simmer uncovered for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the saag has darkened slightly from its electric green to a richer forest green and has thickened to the consistency of a pourable sauce. Season with salt. Stir in the garam masala and swirl in the cream or yogurt — the dairy tempers the sharpness and adds body. If using yogurt, lower the heat to minimum before adding to prevent curdling. The sauce should now taste fully seasoned, warmly spiced, and rich without heaviness.

In a separate small pan, heat 1 tablespoon of ghee over medium-high heat. Add the paneer cubes in a single layer — they should sizzle immediately on contact with the fat. Let them sit undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottom face is golden, then flip each cube and repeat on the adjacent side. You are only browning the surface — the interior of paneer does not need cooking, only the exterior needs color and a slight crust to help it hold its shape in the sauce. Work in batches if your pan is small. Drain on a paper towel.

Gently fold the golden paneer cubes into the hot saag sauce, being careful not to break the cubes. Turn the heat to low and let the paneer warm through in the sauce for 3–4 minutes — this allows the cheese to absorb the spiced sauce at the surface while remaining firm at the center. Do not boil the sauce after adding paneer, as high heat will make it rubbery. Taste the final dish for salt. Serve with a final swirl of cream or a small knob of butter over the top, accompanied by gluten-free flatbread, gluten-free flatbread, or steamed basmati.
fr-saffron-rice: Place the basmati rice in a large bowl. Dissolve 15 g of salt in 1 liter of cold water and pour over the rice — the water should be as salty as the sea; this salting firms the grain structure and prevents the rice from becoming mushy in later steps. Soak for a minimum of 30 minutes and ideally 1 hour. Soaking allows the grain to hydrate slowly and evenly so the parboiling step can cook the outside while the center remains firm. Drain and rinse gently with cold water.

Crush the saffron threads between fingertips or in a small mortar to a fine powder — whole threads release color and flavor incompletely. Place the saffron powder in a small glass or cup. Pour 60 ml of water that is just off the boil (not violently boiling — around 90°C) over the saffron. Stir once and cover the cup. Let steep for a minimum of 15 minutes. The water will turn a deep, glowing amber-orange and smell of hay, honey, and something metallic and floral. This bloomed saffron is used in two places: mixed into the tahdig, and drizzled over the finished rice.

Bring a large pot of water to a vigorous rolling boil — use at least 2 liters of water for 400 g of rice; Persian rice demands space to move freely. Add the remaining salt (10 g). Add the drained rice and stir gently once. Boil uncovered for exactly 5-7 minutes. Test the rice by removing a grain and biting it in half: the outside should be fully cooked and soft, but a small white line should still be visible at the center — the grain is two-thirds cooked. This is the parboil stage. Drain immediately and run cold water over the rice for 15 seconds to stop cooking.

Pour the oil into a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (non-stick or well-seasoned) and heat over medium heat. In a bowl, mix 3 large spoonfuls of parboiled rice with the yogurt, half the saffron water, and turmeric if using — this is the tahdig mixture. Spread it in a thin, even layer across the bottom of the hot oil. Listen: it should sizzle gently. Now pile the remaining rice on top in a pyramid shape — do not press down. Make 5-6 holes through the mound with the handle of a spoon to allow steam to circulate. Drizzle a thin stream of oil or melted butter over the pyramid.

Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel — the cloth absorbs condensation and prevents water droplets from falling back onto the rice, which would make it wet rather than fluffy. Place the lid on tightly. Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes (this starts the tahdig crisping), then reduce to the lowest possible heat and cook for 40-45 minutes without lifting the lid. To unmold: place the pot on a cold, damp cloth or a pot holder for 2 minutes — the thermal shock helps release the tahdig. Remove the lid, place a large flat platter firmly over the pot, and flip in one confident movement. The tahdig should slide out golden and intact onto the platter. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the white rice.
fr-salt-and-pepper-shrimp: Pat the shrimp completely dry with kitchen paper — any surface moisture will cause the oil to spit violently and prevent the shell from crisping. Toss in the cornstarch to coat very lightly — just enough for a barely-there dusting, not a thick batter. Mix in half the salt, white pepper, and the five-spice.

Heat the oil in a wok over the highest possible heat to 190 C (375 F). Fry the shrimp in batches — 8–10 at a time — for exactly 60–75 seconds. The shells will sizzle aggressively and turn bright orange-red. Remove with a spider and drain on a rack. Do not over-fry — the shrimp continue cooking from residual heat.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving about 1 tablespoon in the wok. Return to high heat. Add the garlic, most of the spring onion, and sliced chilli. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and fragrant. Add the fried shrimp back to the wok and toss furiously for 30 seconds to coat with the aromatic mixture. Season with remaining salt and white pepper. Drizzle with sesame oil and toss once more. Serve immediately, garnished with remaining spring onion.
fr-salt-and-pepper-squid: Open the squid tubes and score the inside surface in a crosshatch pattern at 5mm intervals — this gives the starch something to grip and helps the squid curl dramatically in the oil. Cut into 4cm pieces. Keep tentacles whole. Dry everything very thoroughly with paper towels.

Combine potato starch, salt, white pepper, and Sichuan pepper in a bowl. Add the dried squid and toss to coat completely. Shake off excess in a sieve — you want a thin, even coating that barely obscures the squid, not a heavy cloak.

Heat oil to 200 C (390 F) in a wok or deep pan — higher than most frying, because squid is wet. Fry in small batches for exactly 90 seconds. The squid will curl and the coating will set. Do not stir for the first 30 seconds so the crust can form. Remove to a rack — immediately.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving a thin slick. Over high flame, add garlic, chili, and spring onion. Stir-fry for 20–30 seconds until fragrant and the garlic is barely golden. Add the fried squid back and toss furiously for 15 seconds — just enough to perfume the crust without steaming it soft.
fr-salt-baked-branzino: Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F). In a large bowl, combine the coarse sea salt with the egg whites. Mix firmly with your hands until every grain of salt is coated and the mixture resembles wet sand — it should clump when squeezed and hold an impression of your fist. This is the mortar that will seal the fish. If it crumbles and won't hold a shape, add a fourth egg white.

Check the fish cavity is clean and dry. Season the interior lightly with a pinch of salt. Lay the lemon rounds in a shingle pattern along the cavity floor. Pack the fennel fronds, thyme, and parsley in on top of the lemon — the cavity should be visibly full. The herbs will steam inside the crust and perfume the flesh from the inside out without penetrating it externally at all.

Spread a third of the salt mixture onto a rimmed baking sheet in the exact shape and size of the fish, about 1.5 cm thick. Lay the stuffed branzino on top. Pack the remaining salt mixture firmly over the top and sides of the fish, pressing and smoothing it into a solid, even casing at least 1.5 cm thick at every point. Pay special attention to the head and tail — cracks there will let steam escape and dry the flesh. The fish should be completely invisible under the crust. Smooth the surface with wet palms.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 25–30 minutes for a 600g fish. The timing scales with fish weight: add 5 minutes per additional 200g. The crust will harden to a rigid, chalky shell and may develop faint ivory-to-beige colouring on top. It will not brown dramatically — the visual cues here are all about the crust hardening. A probe thermometer inserted through the crust should read 58–60°C at the thickest part of the fish. If you do not have a probe, use the timing as your guide.

Bring the baking sheet to the table. Using the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, crack the crust firmly along the spine of the fish. It will fracture in large shards — peel these away and discard. Carefully lift the top fillet free, then remove the spine in one piece. The bottom fillet sits on the lower salt bed — slide a spatula underneath to lift it clean. Serve the fillets on warmed plates with a generous pour of extra-virgin olive oil and the lemon slices from inside the cavity.
fr-salt-baked-sea-bass: Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F) with a rack in the centre position. Pat the sea bass completely dry — inside the cavity and all over the outside — with multiple changes of paper towels. Dryness is critical: any moisture on the fish surface will steam inside the salt crust rather than allowing the fish to cook in the dry residual heat of the crust. Inspect the fish for any remaining scales by running a finger from tail to head — any that remain will prevent the crust from sealing properly and can embed in the fish.

Lay the ginger slices in an overlapping layer along the length of the cavity floor. Place the knotted scallions on top of the ginger, and tuck the cilantro sprigs around them. Drizzle the Shaoxing wine into the cavity — it will perfume the fish as it steams. Close the cavity by pressing the sides of the fish together gently. The aromatics inside do not season the flesh directly; they create a fragrant steam environment that perfumes the fish from within.

Mix the coarse sea salt and lightly beaten egg whites together with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand that holds its shape when squeezed — it should clump, not crumble. Spread a 1.5cm bed of the salt mixture on a baking tray or oven-proof dish. Lay the stuffed fish on the bed. Pack the remaining salt mixture over and around the entire fish, pressing firmly to build a uniform crust 2cm thick on all sides. Seal any gaps, especially around the tail and head. Bake at 200°C for 25–30 minutes (about 20 minutes per 500g of fish weight, plus 5 minutes for the crust).

At the table, present the salt-crusted dish. Using the back of a heavy spoon or small hammer, crack the crust along the spine with a few firm blows. Lift off the large pieces of crust — the fish skin will often come away with the top crust, revealing bright, pearlescent white flesh beneath. Brush away any salt granules clinging to the flesh with a pastry brush. The fish will not taste salty — the salt crust seasons it only from the outside through the skin, not into the flesh.

Working quickly so the fish does not cool, drizzle the soy sauce evenly over the exposed flesh, followed by the toasted sesame oil — the sesame oil should sizzle faintly as it hits the hot fish. Serve directly from the dish with steamed white jasmine rice and a simple stir-fried green vegetable. Use a tablespoon to scoop portions of the flesh off the spine, keeping the segments as large and intact as possible — this fish deserves to be eaten in generous, moist chunks, not shredded.

fr-salt-cod-brandade: Place the salt cod skin-side up in a large bowl or deep baking dish and cover with cold water. Refrigerate for 24 hours, changing the water at least 3 times — every 6–8 hours is ideal. The water will turn white and cloudy each time, carrying away the curing salt. After the final soak, taste a thin flake from the thickest part: it should taste pleasantly salty, like a well-seasoned fish, not briny or harsh. If it is still harsh, soak 2 more hours.

Place the desalted cod in a wide pan and cover with fresh cold water. Add the thyme. Bring slowly to a bare simmer — tiny bubbles rising at the edges, the water trembling but not boiling. Poach for 10–12 minutes. Do not boil: boiling at this stage firms the protein into a tough, rubbery slab and breaks the fine flakes. The cod is done when it flakes easily along its natural seams when prodded with a fork. Lift out, discard the poaching water, and let it cool enough to handle.

Remove all skin and bones from the cod — run your fingers carefully through the flakes to find every pin bone. Place the cod and raw garlic in a mortar and pound to a paste, or pulse in a food processor. The goal is to break the fish down into a fine, cohesive mass that will absorb the oil and milk. Do not process to a completely smooth paste yet — a slightly grainy, textured base is correct at this stage. The garlic should be fully incorporated and invisible.

With the cod paste in the mortar or a bowl set over gentle heat (or in a stand mixer with paddle), begin adding the warm olive oil in a thin, slow stream, working it in constantly — exactly like making a mayonnaise. When half the oil is incorporated, add a tablespoon of warm milk. Alternate oil and milk until both are fully incorporated. The brandade will transform from a dense paste to a smooth, fluffy, ivory-white emulsion that is light enough to scoop but rich enough to mound. Season with white pepper and lemon juice. Taste: it should be salty, rich, faintly fishy, and deeply satisfying.
fr-salt-crusted-fish: Whisk egg whites to a light foam — no stiff peaks, just broken and fluid. Pour over coarse salt and work with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand. It should clump when squeezed and hold the shape of your fist. If it won't clump, add water a tablespoon at a time.

Preheat oven to 220 C (425 F). Spread a 1.5 cm layer of salt paste on a baking sheet to form the bed. Stuff the fish cavity with thyme, lemon rounds, and garlic. Lay the fish on the salt bed. Pack remaining salt paste firmly over the entire fish, including head and tail, sealing all seams. Press to compact.

Roast for 25-30 minutes for a 700 g fish. The crust will set and begin to show faint golden spots on its highest points. An instant-read thermometer inserted through the crust into the thickest part of the fish should read 55-60 C (130-140 F). The fish steams inside its own armor.

At the table, crack the crust with the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, following the line of the fish's spine. Lift away the top half of the crust in large pieces — it comes off in satisfying slabs. Brush away any salt crystals with a pastry brush. Peel back the skin and serve the fillets with olive oil and lemon wedges. The flesh will be luminous, juicy, and perfectly seasoned.
fr-saltimbocca: Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using the flat face of a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound with firm, even strokes from the center outward — not vertical blows that tear the meat, but angled slides that stretch the fibers. Target 5–6 mm thickness, roughly even across the whole escalope. Season lightly with white pepper only — the prosciutto will provide all the salt needed.

Lay 2–3 sage leaves flat on the top (smooth) side of each escalope. Drape one or two slices of prosciutto over to cover the sage and the entire escalope surface — the ham must extend slightly beyond the meat edges. Secure with one or two wooden toothpicks pierced at an angle through ham, sage, and meat. Season the underside (veal side) very lightly with salt only. Dust the veal side in gluten-free flour and pat off all excess — you want a gossamer coating, not a thick crust.

Heat a large stainless or carbon steel pan over medium-high heat. Add butter and let it foam and subside — when the first wisps of color appear in the butter, it is ready. Place escalopes prosciutto-side down. Press them flat with a spatula for the first 10 seconds to ensure full contact. Cook prosciutto-side for 2–3 minutes until the ham crackles and has rendered its fat into the butter. Flip and cook the veal side for just 60–90 seconds — veal is lean and overcooks in moments.

Remove the escalopes to a warm plate. Over high heat, pour the wine into the still-hot pan and immediately scrape up the browned bits from the base — these are the flavor. Let the wine reduce by half, about 90 seconds of vigorous bubbling. Remove from heat, add a cold knob of butter, and swirl constantly until the sauce becomes glossy and emulsified. Pour over the escalopes immediately. The dish is best eaten within 3 minutes of plating.
fr-samosa-filling: Cover the whole, unpeeled potatoes with cold water in a pot. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook until a thin knife slides through the center with zero resistance — about 20–25 minutes depending on size. Do not rush with high heat or the skins will split and the potatoes will absorb too much water. Drain and immediately peel while hot — the skins slip off easily and the potato flesh sheds moisture better when peeled warm. Spread the peeled potatoes on a tray and leave them uncovered for 5 minutes to steam-dry. Then roughly crush them with a fork or your hands into a mix of small chunks and larger broken pieces. Do not mash smooth — the filling needs texture. Some pieces of potato 1–2 cm across are desirable.

Heat the oil or ghee in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds and crushed coriander seeds together — they should sizzle immediately and begin crackling. Let them bloom for about 30–40 seconds until the cumin turns a deep chestnut brown. Do not stop here — add the minced ginger and green chili and stir for 1 minute until the raw ginger smell softens to a sweet, fragrant note. Add the ground coriander, amchur, garam masala, and turmeric. Stir constantly for 60 seconds, scraping the bottom — the ground spices will form a thick, fragrant paste in the fat. This step, called the tadka or bhuna, is critical: the oil carries fat-soluble spice compounds directly into the potato and peas at the moment of contact. If your spice paste smells warm and rounded, with no raw edge, it is ready.

Add the frozen or fresh peas directly to the spiced fat in the pan. Stir and cook for 2 minutes — the peas will warm through and absorb the spiced oil. Add the crushed potatoes all at once and fold everything together using a wide spatula or wooden spoon, working from the bottom of the pan and turning the mixture over itself. You want to evenly coat every piece of potato and pea in the spice blend without turning the mixture into a smooth mash — the filling should retain texture, with visible pieces of potato and peas throughout. Season with salt and stir. Off the heat, fold in the fresh cilantro. Taste: the filling should be intensely flavored — boldly salty, bright with amchur's sour note, and warmly spiced throughout. It needs to be seasoned aggressively because the gluten-free pastry shell will dilute the intensity. Allow the filling to cool completely before enclosing in gluten-free pastry — warm filling will steam the gluten-free pastry and make it soggy.
